questions.stem: Which of the following is a field of chemistry?
explanation_steps: Chemistry is divided into branches: organic, inorganic, physical, analytical, biochemistry, industrial and nuclear chemistry, among others.
All four options are fields of chemistry. Answer: E.
tips: Organic = carbon compounds; biochemistry = chemistry of living things; nuclear = chemistry of the nucleus; industrial = large-scale production.

similar_questions.stem: The branch of chemistry that studies the chemical processes in living organisms is
explanation_steps: Biochemistry deals with the chemistry of living things (proteins, enzymes, DNA). Answer: B.

questions.stem: The correct chemical symbol for an atom of the element carbon is
explanation_steps: Carbon's symbol is the single capital letter C.
Ca = calcium, Cr = chromium, Co = cobalt; 'Cb' is not a current symbol. Answer: C.
tips: A symbol is one capital letter, or a capital followed by a small letter: Co (cobalt) ≠ CO (carbon monoxide).

similar_questions.stem: Which symbol represents cobalt?
explanation_steps: Cobalt = Co (capital C, small o); CO is the compound carbon monoxide; Cu is copper. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The atomic number is the number of ______ in the nucleus of each atom of a specific element.
explanation_steps: The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus; it identifies the element.
Electrons are outside the nucleus (their number equals Z only in a neutral atom); neutrons + protons give the mass number. Answer: B.
tips: Z = protons; A = protons + neutrons.

similar_questions.stem: An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons. Its mass number is
explanation_steps: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about Mendeleev's Periodic Table?

options.A: It classifies elements into groups and periods.
options.B: It predicts the existence of undiscovered elements.
options.C: It has gaps in the periodic table.
options.D: It indicates clearly the position of hydrogen.
options.E: It has irregular arrangement for some pairs of elements.

explanation_steps: Mendeleev arranged elements in groups and periods, left gaps and predicted undiscovered elements (e.g. eka-silicon = germanium) – A, B, C are true.

Among its defects: the position of hydrogen was not clear (it resembles both alkali metals and halogens), isotopes had no place, and some pairs were out of mass order (irregular pairs) – so E is true.
'It indicates clearly the position of hydrogen' is false. Answer: D.
tips: Defects of Mendeleev's table: hydrogen's position, isotopes, anomalous pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I).

similar_questions.stem: Which was a merit (strength) of Mendeleev's periodic table?

options.A: It fixed the position of hydrogen
options.B: It had a place for isotopes
options.C: It left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties
options.D: All elements were in increasing atomic mass order
options.E: It was based on atomic number

explanation_steps: Leaving gaps and predicting properties of gallium, scandium and germanium was his main success. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1 Mendeleev's periodic table – merits and limitations

questions.stem: A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature is called
explanation_steps: An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute.
A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that the solvent can dissolve at that temperature – no more dissolves.
A supersaturated solution holds MORE than the saturated amount (unstable), prepared by cooling a hot saturated solution. Answer: C.
tips: Unsaturated < saturated (maximum, in equilibrium with undissolved solid) < supersaturated (unstable excess).

similar_questions.stem: A crystal added to a solution dissolves. The solution was
explanation_steps: Only an unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about basic solutions? They
explanation_steps: Bases turn red litmus blue, feel slippery (soapy), have pH > 7 and neutralise acids.
A sour taste is a property of ACIDS; bases taste bitter. Answer: D.
tips: Acid: sour, red litmus, pH < 7. Base: bitter, slippery, blue litmus, pH > 7.

similar_questions.stem: Which property belongs to acids?
explanation_steps: Acids taste sour (lemon, vinegar). Answer: D.

questions.stem: The stored chemical energy in a molecule is a kind of ______ energy.
explanation_steps: Energy is kinetic (energy of motion: thermal, electrical, sound) or potential (stored energy of position or composition).
Chemical energy is stored in the bonds of molecules and released during reactions – it is potential energy. Answer: B.
tips: Stored energy (chemical, gravitational, elastic) = potential; energy of motion = kinetic.

similar_questions.stem: The energy stored in a battery before it is used is mainly
explanation_steps: A battery stores chemical (potential) energy that is converted to electrical energy. Answer: B.

questions.stem: In oxidation-reduction reactions, oxidation involves

options.A: an addition of oxygen to a substance.
options.B: a loss of electron(s) from a substance.
options.C: a removal of hydrogen from a substance.

explanation_steps: The textbook gives several equivalent definitions of oxidation: addition of oxygen, removal of hydrogen, loss of electrons and increase in oxidation number.
All four statements describe oxidation. Answer: E.
tips: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain.

similar_questions.stem: Which change is a reduction?
explanation_steps: Gain of electrons (Cu²⁺ → Cu, oxidation number +2 → 0) is reduction. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common form of amorphous carbon?
explanation_steps: The textbook lists the common forms of amorphous carbon: 1. coke (coal heated without air), 2. wood charcoal, 3. animal charcoal (from bones), 4. carbon black (lampblack).
All four options are amorphous carbon. Answer: E.
tips: Crystalline allotropes: diamond, graphite, fullerene. Amorphous forms: coke, charcoal, carbon black (soot).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a crystalline allotrope of carbon?
explanation_steps: Graphite (like diamond and fullerene) is crystalline; the others are amorphous. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The property "metallic luster" of metals refers to the ______ of metals.
explanation_steps: Lustre is the shine of a freshly cut or polished metal surface.
Malleability = hammered into sheets; ductility = drawn into wires; conductivity = passes heat/electricity; the ringing sound is sonority. Answer: A.
tips: Lustrous = shiny; malleable = sheets; ductile = wires; sonorous = rings when struck.

similar_questions.stem: The property that allows copper to be drawn into thin wires is
explanation_steps: Drawing into wires = ductility. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about the properties of gases? They
explanation_steps: Gas particles are far apart with large empty spaces between them, so gases expand to fill any container, are easily compressed and diffuse rapidly.
Because there is so much empty space, gases have LOW density (about 1000 times less than liquids). Answer: D.
tips: Gases: expand, compress, diffuse, low density.

similar_questions.stem: Gases are easily compressed because

options.B: there are large spaces between their particles

explanation_steps: Large empty spaces between gas molecules allow them to be pushed closer. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is not a crystalline solid?
explanation_steps: Crystalline solids have a regular, repeating arrangement of particles and sharp melting points: sugar, sulphur, NaCl and diamond.
Glass is an amorphous solid – its particles are arranged irregularly and it softens over a range of temperatures. Answer: D.
tips: Amorphous examples: glass, plastic, rubber, amorphous carbon.

similar_questions.stem: Which property is typical of an amorphous solid?

options.C: Softens gradually over a temperature range

explanation_steps: Amorphous solids lack long-range order, so they soften gradually. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Pentanal belongs to the class of organic compounds called
explanation_steps: IUPAC names of aldehydes end in '-al' (–CHO group): methanal, ethanal, … pentanal = CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CHO.
Ketones end in -one, alcohols in -ol, acids in -oic acid. Answer: B.
tips: -al = aldehyde, -one = ketone, -ol = alcohol, -oic acid = carboxylic acid.

similar_questions.stem: Propanone (acetone) belongs to
explanation_steps: The ending -one indicates a ketone. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Nuclear reactions
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 3.1 compares chemical and nuclear reactions: nuclear reactions involve the nucleus (protons and neutrons), involve very large energy changes, involve loss of mass (converted to energy) and are irreversible.
All four statements are correct. Answer: E.
tips: Chemical reactions: electrons, small energy, no mass loss, often reversible. Nuclear: nucleons, huge energy, mass loss, irreversible.

similar_questions.stem: Which statement is true of chemical (not nuclear) reactions?

options.A: They involve changes in the nucleus
options.B: They convert mass into large amounts of energy
options.C: They involve the rearrangement of electrons
options.D: Their rate is unaffected by temperature

explanation_steps: Chemical reactions only involve valence electrons. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The direct change of a solid into a gas is said to be
explanation_steps: Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state (iodine, dry ice, naphthalene).
Melting: solid → liquid; freezing: liquid → solid; evaporation: liquid → gas; condensation: gas → liquid. Answer: D.
tips: The reverse of sublimation (gas → solid) is deposition.

similar_questions.stem: Which substance sublimes when heated?
explanation_steps: Iodine crystals turn directly into violet vapour. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about an atom of an element?

options.A: All matter is composed of different types of atoms.
options.B: Atoms are far too small to be seen with the naked eye.
options.C: The protons and neutrons are found in the nucleus of an atom.
options.D: Together the protons and neutrons are called nucleons.

explanation_steps: All matter is made of atoms of the different elements (Dalton) – A; atoms are far too small to see – B.
Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus – C – and are together called nucleons – D.
All statements are correct. Answer: E.
tips: Nucleons = protons + neutrons; their number is the mass number.

similar_questions.stem: The total number of nucleons in ²³Na (Z = 11) is
explanation_steps: Nucleons = mass number = 23. Answer: C.

questions.stem: All of the following are properties of non-metals, except that they
explanation_steps: Non-metals tend to gain electrons forming anions (Cl⁻, O²⁻); solid non-metals are brittle and dull (non-lustrous).
Malleability (can be hammered into sheets) is a property of METALS. Answer: B.
tips: Non-metal solids (sulphur, iodine, carbon) crumble – they are brittle, not malleable.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a property of metals but not of non-metals?
explanation_steps: Malleability is typical of metals. Answer: D.

questions.stem: One of the following pairs has elements in different groups of the periodic table. [At. No: Li = 3, N = 7, F = 9, Na = 11, Mg = 12, P = 15, Cl = 17, K = 19]
explanation_steps: Group = number of valence electrons: Li (2,1) → group 1; F (2,7) → group 17 (VII).
Na (2,8,1)/K (2,8,8,1) both group 1; Mg/Ca both group 2; N (2,5)/P (2,8,5) both group 15; Cl/F both group 17.
Only Li and F are in different groups. Answer: D.
tips: Same number of valence electrons → same group; same number of shells → same period.

similar_questions.stem: Which pair is in the same period? [Z: Li 3, Na 11, O 8, S 16, F 9]
explanation_steps: Li (2,1) and F (2,7) both have 2 shells → period 2. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following properties is not a colligative property of a solution?
explanation_steps: Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles, not their identity: vapour-pressure lowering, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and osmotic pressure.
Colour depends on the identity of the solute. Answer: D.
tips: Four colligative properties: vapour-pressure lowering, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression, osmotic pressure.

similar_questions.stem: Adding salt to water
explanation_steps: Dissolved particles depress the freezing point (and raise the boiling point, lower vapour pressure). Answer: D.

questions.stem: A solution that has a pH of 7 is
explanation_steps: pH < 7 acidic, pH = 7 neutral ([H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ M at 25 °C), pH > 7 basic. Answer: C.
tips: Pure water at 25 °C has pH 7.

similar_questions.stem: A solution with pH 3 is
explanation_steps: pH below 7 is acidic. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Which of the following covalent bonds has the highest bond energy?
explanation_steps: More shared electron pairs between the same two atoms → stronger bond.
Typical bond energies (kJ/mol): C–C 348, C–O 360, C–H 413, C=C 614, C≡C ≈ 839.
The triple bond C≡C is strongest. Answer: D.
tips: Bond strength: triple > double > single (for the same pair of atoms).

similar_questions.stem: Which bond is weakest?
explanation_steps: Single bonds are weakest; C–C (348 kJ/mol). Answer: D.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide is useful during the following processes, except

options.A: in the bottling of mineral water.
options.C: as a refrigerant for ice cream.

explanation_steps: The textbook's uses of CO₂: plant life (photosynthesis), refrigeration (dry ice – ice cream and meat), beverages (bottling of mineral water and soft drinks) and fire extinguishers.
Making fertilizers is not among the listed uses, so B is the intended answer. Answer: B.
tips: Remember four textbook uses of CO₂: photosynthesis, dry ice, fizzy drinks, fire extinguishers.

similar_questions.stem: Solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) is used
explanation_steps: Dry ice sublimes at −78 °C and is used for refrigeration. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: B is keyed because fertilizer-making is not in the textbook's list of CO₂ uses (p.80). Industrially, however, CO₂ is a raw material for urea fertilizer (2NH₃ + CO₂ → CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O), so B is not strictly false. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following metals does not react with water at any conditions?
explanation_steps: K and Na react vigorously with cold water; Ca reacts less violently with cold water.
Aluminium does not react with cold or hot water but reacts with steam.
The textbook: 'Metals such as lead, copper, silver, gold and platinum do not react with water at all.' Answer: C.
tips: Water: K, Na, Ca (cold) > Mg (hot) > Al, Zn, Fe (steam) > Pb, Cu, Ag, Au, Pt (none).

similar_questions.stem: Which metal reacts with steam but not with cold water?
explanation_steps: Iron reacts with steam: 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following represents a chemical change?

options.A: Separation of iron from sulphur by a magnet
options.B: Filtering sand from sodium chloride solution

explanation_steps: A chemical change produces new substances with new properties and is not easily reversed.
Magnetic separation, filtration, melting ice and dissolving sugar are physical changes.
Frying an egg changes (denatures) the proteins irreversibly – a chemical change. Answer: E.
tips: Signs of a chemical change: new substance, colour change, gas, heat/light, irreversibility.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a physical change?
explanation_steps: Melting changes only the state. Answer: D.

questions.stem: The gas law that describes the relation between volume and the number of moles at constant temperature and pressure is called
explanation_steps: Boyle: V vs P (T, n constant). Charles: V vs T (P, n constant).
Avogadro's law: at constant T and P, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to the number of moles (V = kn). Answer: C.
tips: Equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules (Avogadro).

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Carbon monoxide is an odourless, tasteless and colourless gas' – so A and C are false (it burns with a blue flame, but the gas is colourless).
CO does not turn lime water milky – that is the test for CO₂.
'Carbon monoxide is a good reducing agent': PbO + CO → Pb + CO₂. Answer: D.
tips: CO: colourless, odourless, poisonous, neutral, reducing agent, burns with a blue flame.

similar_questions.stem: Which gas turns lime water milky?

questions.stem: All of the following are radioactive decays, except
explanation_steps: Radioactive decay is the spontaneous emission of α particles, β particles or γ rays from an unstable nucleus.
Ionisation of sodium (Na → Na⁺ + e⁻) removes a valence electron – a chemical change that does not involve the nucleus. Answer: B.
tips: Radioactivity = nucleus changes; ionisation = electrons change.

similar_questions.stem: Which radiation has no mass and no charge?
explanation_steps: Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation. Answer: C.

explanation_steps: Sodium is a typical alkali metal: soft (cut with a knife), malleable, a good conductor and very reactive (stored under kerosene).
Brittleness is a property of non-metals, not of sodium. Answer: D.
tips: Alkali metals: soft, low density, very reactive, stored under oil.

questions.stem: A process in which a very heavy metal nucleus splits into more stable nuclei is called
explanation_steps: Fission: a heavy nucleus (e.g. U-235 after absorbing a neutron) splits into two lighter, more stable nuclei with release of neutrons and a large amount of energy.
Fusion joins light nuclei. Answer: A.
tips: Fission = splitting (nuclear reactors); fusion = joining (the Sun).

similar_questions.stem: The energy of the Sun comes from
explanation_steps: Hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium in the Sun. Answer: B.

questions.stem: If a gas expands at constant temperature, the

options.A: number of molecules of the gas decreases.
options.B: kinetic energy of the molecules decreases.
options.C: kinetic energy of the molecules remains constant.
options.D: kinetic energy of the molecules increases.

explanation_steps: By kinetic molecular theory, the average kinetic energy of gas molecules is proportional to the absolute temperature only.
At constant temperature the average kinetic energy is constant, whatever the volume; the number of molecules also does not change. Answer: C.
tips: KEₐvg ∝ T (kelvin) – volume and pressure do not change it.

similar_questions.stem: If the absolute temperature of a gas is doubled, the average kinetic energy of its molecules
explanation_steps: KE ∝ T, so doubling T doubles KE. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The separation of a mixture into its constituents in a pure form is based on the

options.C: acidic or basic nature of the constituents.

explanation_steps: Separation methods exploit a difference in some property of the components.

Particle size → filtration/sieving; boiling point → distillation; colour → hand picking (the Grade 9 activity separates sulphur and iron by colour); acidic/basic nature → dissolving one component in acid or base.
Every listed property can be the basis of a separation, so 'All of the above' is the intended answer. Answer: E.
tips: Choose the method by the difference: size (filter), boiling point (distil), magnetism (magnet), solubility (dissolve + filter), volatility (sublime/evaporate).

similar_questions.stem: A mixture of alcohol (b.p. 78 °C) and water (b.p. 100 °C) is best separated by
explanation_steps: The difference in boiling points is used in fractional distillation. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The equation for the equilibrium constant Kc = [C]²/([A][B]²) is correct for the reaction
explanation_steps: For aA + bB ⇌ cC, Kc = [C]ᶜ/([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ): each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient.
The expression has [A]¹, [B]² and [C]², so a = 1, b = 2, c = 2: A + 2B ⇌ 2C. Answer: C.
tips: Products on top, reactants below, coefficients become exponents.

similar_questions.stem: Write Kc for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
explanation_steps: Exponents equal the coefficients: [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³). Answer: B.

questions.stem: The process in which heavier fractions of petroleum are converted into lighter gasoline fractions (e.g., C₁₆H₃₄ → C₉H₂₀ + C₇H₁₄) is called
explanation_steps: Cracking breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller ones (an alkane and an alkene) by heat and a catalyst, increasing the yield of gasoline.
Fractional distillation only separates by boiling point; polymerisation joins molecules; esterification makes esters; saponification makes soap. Answer: C.
tips: Cracking: big → small (alkane + alkene). Polymerisation: small → big.

similar_questions.stem: Balance the cracking: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + ?
explanation_steps: Atoms left: C 10−8 = 2, H 22−18 = 4 → C₂H₄ (ethene). Answer: B.

explanation_steps: The configuration depends on the atomic number (20 electrons in the neutral atom), not on the mass number 40.
Filling shells: 2, 8, 8, then the 4s shell takes the last 2 → 2, 8, 8, 2 (calcium). Answer: E.
tips: For Z ≤ 20: 2, 8, 8, then remaining electrons in the 4th shell.

similar_questions.stem: The electron configuration of ³⁹₁₉K is
explanation_steps: 19 electrons: 2, 8, 8, 1. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following properties refers to sulphuric acid?

options.C: It is a good reducing agent.

explanation_steps: Sulphuric acid is a strong acid (not weak), a dense oily liquid (≈1.84 g/cm³), an oxidising and dehydrating agent (not a reducing agent) and, like all acids, sour (bitter is typical of bases).
Concentrated H₂SO₄ is highly corrosive – it chars sugar, paper and skin. Answer: E.
tips: Always add acid to water, never water to acid.

similar_questions.stem: When concentrated H₂SO₄ is added to sugar, a black mass forms because the acid acts as a
explanation_steps: It removes H₂O from C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ leaving carbon. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The positively charged polyatomic ion is
explanation_steps: Ammonium NH₄⁺ is a positively charged polyatomic ion.
Dichromate Cr₂O₇²⁻, permanganate MnO₄⁻ and nitrite NO₂⁻ are polyatomic but negative.
Ferrous ion Fe²⁺ is positive but monatomic. Answer: A.
tips: NH₄⁺ (and H₃O⁺) are the common positive polyatomic ions; most others are anions.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a polyatomic anion?
explanation_steps: Sulphate contains several atoms and a negative charge. Answer: C.

questions.stem: When moving across a period from left to right in the periodic table, the

options.A: ionization energy of the elements decreases.
options.B: metallic character of the elements increases.
options.C: non-metallic character of the elements decreases.
options.D: atomic size of the elements increases.

explanation_steps: Across a period the nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, so atoms get smaller and hold electrons more tightly.
Therefore ionisation energy increases, metallic character decreases, non-metallic character increases, atomic size decreases and electronegativity increases.
Only E is correct. Answer: E.
tips: Across → : size ↓, IE ↑, EN ↑, metallic ↓. Down ↓ : size ↑, IE ↓, EN ↓, metallic ↑.

similar_questions.stem: Which element of period 3 has the largest atomic radius?
explanation_steps: Radius decreases across the period, so Na is largest. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Which of the following group lists all substances with fixed chemical composition and definite proportion?
explanation_steps: Only pure substances (elements and compounds) have fixed composition and definite proportion.
Water (H₂O), oxygen (O₂) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) are all pure substances.
Each other group contains a mixture: amalgam, air, sea water, soda water, steel, milk, petrol, tea. Answer: B.
tips: Law of definite proportions: a compound always has the same elements in the same mass ratio (water: 1 g H : 8 g O).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a mixture?
explanation_steps: Brass is an alloy (Cu + Zn) of variable composition. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following mixtures is an example of a liquid solution?
explanation_steps: Solutions are classified by the state of the final solution (the solvent).
Air is a gaseous solution; steel, brass and bronze are solid solutions (alloys).
Sea water (salts dissolved in water) is a liquid solution. Answer: C.
tips: Alloys = solid solutions; air = gaseous solution; soda water, sea water, vinegar = liquid solutions.

similar_questions.stem: Brass is an example of a
explanation_steps: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc – a solid solution. Answer: C.

questions.stem: An oxidizing agent can be described as a substance that
explanation_steps: An oxidising agent takes electrons from another substance, so it causes that substance to be oxidised.
By gaining electrons, the oxidising agent is itself reduced.
Only B is fully correct ('gains electrons and causes oxidation'). C is wrong because gaining electrons is reduction, not oxidation. Answer: B.
tips: Oxidising agent: gains e⁻, is reduced, causes oxidation. Reducing agent: loses e⁻, is oxidised, causes reduction.

similar_questions.stem: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, the reducing agent is

questions.image_alt: Energy profile (energy on the vertical axis labelled 5, reaction coordinate horizontal). The reactant level is a flat line; arrow 2 runs from the axis up to it. Arrow 1 goes from the reactant level to the peak; arrow 4 goes from the product level to the peak; short arrow 3 spans the gap between the reactant level (dashed) and the product level.

questions.stem: Mention any three methods used for separating mixtures. (3 points)
questions.answer: Any three of: filtration, evaporation (crystallisation), simple distillation, fractional distillation, decantation, sublimation, magnetic separation, chromatography, separating funnel, hand picking, sieving, centrifugation.

subparts.question: First method
steps: Separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.

subparts.question: Second method
steps: Separates liquids (or a solvent from a solute) by boiling point.

subparts.question: Third method
steps: Recovers a dissolved solid (salt from sea water).

explanation_steps: Separation methods are physical processes that use a difference in a physical property of the components.

Filtration (particle size / solubility – sand from salt water); evaporation or crystallisation (salt from sea water); distillation (boiling point – pure water from salt water); fractional distillation (liquids with close boiling points – alcohol and water); sublimation (iodine or naphthalene from sand); magnetic separation (iron from sulphur); decantation / separating funnel (immiscible liquids – oil and water); chromatography (dyes in ink).
marking_points: Accept any valid method: filtration, evaporation, crystallisation, distillation, fractional distillation, decantation, sublimation, magnetic separation, chromatography, separating funnel, sieving, hand picking, centrifugation
tips: Name the method and, if you can, the property it uses – examiners accept any three correct methods.

questions.stem:
Name the following parts of an atom: (4 points)
2.1 Dense part of the atom
2.2 Circular path of electrons
2.3 The heaviest particle
2.4 The positively charged particle
questions.answer: 2.1 Nucleus; 2.2 Shell (orbit / energy level); 2.3 Neutron; 2.4 Proton.

subparts.question: Dense part of the atom
steps: Contains the protons and neutrons – nearly all the mass.

subparts.question: Circular path of electrons
steps: Bohr's circular orbits K, L, M, N.

subparts.question: The heaviest particle
steps: Slightly heavier than the proton; the electron is ~1/1840 as heavy.

explanation_steps: Almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its tiny, dense nucleus (2.1).
In the Bohr model, electrons move in circular paths called orbits, shells or energy levels (K, L, M…) (2.2).
Of the subatomic particles, the neutron (1.6749 × 10⁻²⁴ g) is slightly heavier than the proton (1.6726 × 10⁻²⁴ g); the electron is about 1/1840 of either (2.3).
The proton carries the positive charge (+1) (2.4).
marking_points: 1 point each: nucleus; shell/orbit/energy level; neutron; proton
2.3: 'neutron' is the precise answer; a teacher may give credit for 'proton' only if the class was taught that p and n have equal mass
tips: Masses: neutron ≳ proton ≫ electron. Charges: proton +1, electron −1, neutron 0.

steps: Balanced: 2 Cu and 2 O on each side.

explanation_steps: Calcium ion Ca²⁺; sulphite SO₃²⁻; sulphate SO₄²⁻. Equal and opposite charges combine 1 : 1 → CaSO₃ and CaSO₄.
Copper(II) oxide: Cu²⁺ + O²⁻ → CuO. Skeleton: Cu + O₂ → CuO; balance O by putting 2 before CuO, then 2 before Cu: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO.

tips: -ite has one O fewer than -ate: sulphite SO₃²⁻, sulphate SO₄²⁻; nitrite NO₂⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻.

questions.stem: A solution is prepared by dissolving 8 g of solute in 40 g of solvent. Calculate the mass percent of the solute in the solution. (2 points)
explanation_steps: Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent = 8 g + 40 g = 48 g.
Mass percent = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100 = (8/48) × 100 = 16.7 %.
Common error: dividing by the solvent only (8/40 × 100 = 20 %) is wrong.
marking_points: 1 point: mass of solution = 48 g (or correct formula)
tips: Always divide by the mass of the whole SOLUTION.

questions.stem:
Define end point and equivalence point. (2 points)
5.1 End point
5.2 Equivalence point
questions.answer: 5.1 End point: the point in a titration at which the indicator changes colour, showing that the titration should stop. 5.2 Equivalence point: the point at which the amount (equivalents/moles) of titrant added is exactly enough to react completely with the substance being titrated (acid and base exactly neutralise each other).

subparts.question: End point
subparts.answer: The point at which the indicator changes colour during a titration.

subparts.question: Equivalence point
subparts.answer: The point at which the reactants have reacted in exactly stoichiometric (equivalent) amounts.
steps: Equivalents of acid = equivalents of base.

explanation_steps: In a titration a solution of known concentration is added from a burette until the reaction is just complete.
The equivalence point is the theoretical point where equivalents of acid = equivalents of base.
The end point is the experimental point where the indicator changes colour; a well-chosen indicator makes the end point very close to the equivalence point.
tips: Equivalence = chemistry (exact stoichiometry); end point = what you see (colour change).

similar_questions.stem: Why is phenolphthalein suitable for titrating NaOH with HCl?
similar_questions.answer: Because it changes colour (pink → colourless) in the pH range around the equivalence point, so its end point practically coincides with the equivalence point.
explanation_steps: An indicator is chosen whose colour change occurs near the equivalence-point pH.

questions.stem: What are isomers? (1 point)
questions.answer: Isomers are compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structural formulas (different arrangements of atoms) and hence different properties.
explanation_steps: Example: C₄H₁₀ exists as butane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ and 2-methylpropane CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃.
They have the same molecular formula but different structures, so different boiling points and other properties.
marking_points: 1 point: same molecular formula AND different structure/arrangement (½ if only one part)
tips: Same formula, different structure.

similar_questions.stem: Draw/name two isomers of C₂H₆O.
similar_questions.answer: Ethanol CH₃CH₂OH and dimethyl ether CH₃OCH₃.
explanation_steps: Both are C₂H₆O but have different functional groups (alcohol vs ether).

questions.stem: Write three differences between exothermic and endothermic reactions. (3 points)
questions.answer: Exothermic: releases heat to the surroundings; ΔH is negative; products have less heat content (enthalpy) than reactants; surroundings get warmer (e.g. combustion, neutralisation). Endothermic: absorbs heat from the surroundings; ΔH is positive; products have more heat content than reactants; surroundings get cooler (e.g. photosynthesis, decomposition of CaCO₃).

explanation_steps: Compare the direction of heat flow, the sign of ΔH, the relative enthalpy of reactants and products, the temperature change of the surroundings, and examples.
marking_points: 1 point for each correct pair of differences (maximum 3)
tips: Exothermic: 'exit' of heat. Endothermic: heat 'enters'.

similar_questions.stem: Classify as exothermic or endothermic: (a) burning of charcoal, (b) melting of ice, (c) photosynthesis, (d) respiration.
explanation_steps: Heat released: burning, respiration. Heat absorbed: melting, photosynthesis.

questions.stem:
Nitrogen is present in the atmosphere in 78 % by volume and is important for all living things. During the nitrogen cycle,
8.1 do organisms use the nitrogen directly from the atmosphere? (1 point)
8.2 what is the advantage of the bacteria present in the soil? (1 point)
questions.answer: 8.1 No – organisms cannot use atmospheric nitrogen directly. 8.2 Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soil (and root nodules of legumes) convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium and nitrate compounds that plants absorb and use to make proteins (denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the air).

subparts.question: Do organisms use nitrogen directly from the atmosphere?
steps: N₂ must first be fixed into compounds.

subparts.question: Advantage of the soil bacteria
subparts.answer: They fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium/nitrate compounds that plants can use to make proteins.

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'organisms cannot use the nitrogen directly from the atmosphere. However, certain bacteria present in the soil and some plants convert the atmospheric nitrogen to ammonium and nitrate compounds. Plants make proteins from these compounds and animals obtain proteins when they eat these plants.'
marking_points: 8.2: 1 point for converting (fixing) atmospheric N₂ into ammonium/nitrate compounds usable by plants
tips: N₂ is very unreactive (N≡N triple bond) – it must be 'fixed' before plants can use it.

similar_questions.stem: Name the process by which bacteria convert N₂ of the air into ammonium compounds, and name the bacteria that return N₂ to the atmosphere.
explanation_steps: Fixation turns N₂ into NH₄⁺/NO₃⁻; denitrification turns nitrates back into N₂.

questions.stem: Mention three uses of aluminum. (3 points)
questions.answer: Any three of: kitchen utensils (cooking pots); aluminium foil for wrapping food; drink cans and packaging; bodies of aircraft, cars, ships and trains (light and strong alloys such as duralumin); overhead electric power cables; window and door frames, roofing sheets; paint (aluminium powder); thermite welding / extraction of other metals.
explanation_steps: Aluminium is light (low density), strong in alloys, a good conductor of heat and electricity, resistant to corrosion (protective Al₂O₃ layer), malleable and ductile.

These properties give its uses: utensils and foil (conducts heat, non-toxic, malleable); aircraft and vehicles (light, strong alloys); power cables (good conductor, light); window frames and cans (corrosion-resistant).
tips: Link each use to a property: light, conductor, corrosion-resistant, malleable.

questions.stem: An inflated balloon has a volume of 4.0 L at 0.8 atm and is allowed to ascend in altitude until the pressure is 0.3 atm. During the ascent the temperature of the gas decreased from 25 °C to 23 °C. Calculate the volume of the balloon at its final altitude. (2 points)
explanation_steps: Use the combined gas law (amount of gas constant): P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
Convert temperatures to kelvin: T₁ = 25 + 273 = 298 K; T₂ = 23 + 273 = 296 K.
Check: pressure falls to less than half → volume more than doubles; slight cooling reduces it a little.
marking_points: 1 point: correct combined gas law with temperatures in kelvin
tips: Always use kelvin in gas-law calculations.
